summary: Launch Logic: Satellite Engineering Game is an interactive, console-based C++ simulation designed for 1 to 4 players that turns complex spacecraft systems engineering into an accessible, collaborative tabletop-style experience. Addressing the challenge of making abstract space mission constraints tangible for students, the game places players in specialized NASA-inspired crew roles—Mission Planner, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms & Launch Officer—to design, configure, and launch orbital missions. Teams must balance strict real-world trade-offs across budget, payload mass, net power, scientific output, orbital lifetime, and data downlink capacity across multiple mission scenarios, including a classified deep-space Europa Ice Probe. By combining role-based accountability with instant diagnostic post-mission reports, Launch Logic empowers students to intuitively grasp how aerospace engineers navigate competing constraints to achieve mission success.
details:
Launch Logic is a lightweight, turn-based C++ engineering simulation game built for 1 to 4 players. At the start of a session, players are assigned four distinct mission control roles:

  1. Mission Planner: Selects the mission scenario and grants final launch authorization.
  2. Systems Engineer: Sets the difficulty level (Cadet or Engineer) and manages solar power arrays and radiation shielding.
  3. Science Lead: Selects scientific payloads (Standard Imager or High-Res Radar) to meet science targets.
  4. Comms & Launch Officer: Manages X-Band downlink bandwidth and initiates the final launch countdown.

Players select from three distinct scenarios: Earth Climate Monitor, Deep Ocean Radar Mapping, or a hidden deep-space challenge—Classified: Europa Ice Probe (unlocked via secret code 99), which introduces harsh Jovian radiation requiring mandatory radiation shielding. In Engineer (Hard) mode, teams also face a $40M budget reduction and a 60W solar storm power drain. Every subsystem installation requires explicit confirmation from the responsible department head. Upon launch, the simulation evaluates all engineering parameters; if a mission fails, a diagnostic Post-Mission Engineering Report pinpoints the exact root cause (e.g., power deficit, downlink bottleneck, or mass overrun) and identifies the responsible department for review before allowing an instant crew replay.

Benefits & Intended Impact Aerospace systems engineering often feels intimidating and overly theoretical to secondary school and early university students. Launch Logic bridges this gap by transforming static physics and engineering equations into dynamic, hands-on decision-making. It fosters teamwork, communication, and systems thinking, helping students understand that maximizing one metric (such as high-resolution scientific data) directly impacts power, mass, and communication bandwidth.

Tools, Languages & Development

  • Programming Language: Standard C++ (<iostream>, <string>, <sstream>), engineered for 100% compatibility with lightweight and legacy educational compilers (such as Dev-C++) so any student can compile and run it without heavy hardware or external libraries.
  • Presentation & Visuals: Canva for pitch deck design and mission workflow visualization.
  • AI/SI Assistance: Large Language Models were used strictly for code debugging, input validation refinement, and text proofreading.

Creativity & Team Considerations Rather than building a single-player calculator, our team (The Budgeteers) designed a cooperative, role-locked workflow where teammates must actively negotiate trade-offs before signing off on hardware. We prioritized accessibility and replayability—implementing robust input validation to prevent crashes, persistent crew rosters across retries, and a hidden deep-space Easter egg (99) to reward curiosity and iterative engineering.
